records.title: Mining the Mekong: Land and Livelihoods Lost to Cambodia’s Thirst for Sand
records.originalTitle: Mining the Mekong: Land and Livelihoods Lost to Cambodia’s Thirst for Sand
records.location: Roka Koang commune, Kandal province, on the Mekong River, Cambodia; also the Bassac River
records.summary: Pulitzer Center story (supported by its Rainforest Investigations Network) reports that residents of Roka Koang commune, Kandal province, blame sand mining by politically connected companies for riverbank collapses on the Mekong that have cost them homes and fishing-based livelihoods. The Cambodian government, via Ung Dipola of the Ministry of Mines and Energy, denies that dredging causes erosion and says it helps stabilise the banks; University of Newcastle and University of Southampton researchers call this "a myth". According to the Ministry of Mines and Energy, Cambodia has 49 active licenses covering 2,320 hectares of the Mekong and Bassac rivers, and 11.7 million m3 of sand was extracted in 2020 and 11.5 million m3 in 2021, with 6.1 million m3 in the first six months of 2022. Dipola said only around 4% of the river is licensed for dredging. Hackney's research suggested extraction exceeded natural replenishment by almost five times in 2018 and by a factor of 16 in 2020. Echo-sounder surveys by Leyland and Darby found extraction scars routinely 5 m deep and one barge taking roughly 9,450 m3 in a day. The researchers warn that riverbed lowering could affect the Tonle Sap reversal of flow. The article also describes company ownership links to political elites, including Global Green Energy Development, Jin Ling Construction and Sophearoth Aphivath, and says the government has not released the environmental impact assessments.
records.limitations: The supplied article text is truncated and ends mid-sentence. Allegations about company links and the official's family ties are attributed to the reporting. Residents' causal claims are disputed by officials. No publisher datePublished metadata was supplied, so the date is taken from the body text. Automated English summary; native-language review may be needed.

records.title: From Tibet to the 'Nine Dragons', the Mekong is losing sand
records.originalTitle: From Tibet to the 'Nine Dragons', the Mekong is losing sand
records.location: Ben Tre province and other Mekong Delta provinces, Vietnam (dateline Mo Cay); also Stung Treng province, Cambodia, mentioned for a dam
records.summary: Reuters reports that upstream damming and extensive mining of the Mekong's riverbed for sand is causing the land in the delta to sink at around 2cm a year, according to experts and officials ("to sink at a pace of around 2cm a year, experts and officials said"). Erosion is destroying homes in Ben Tre province. Can Tho University's Dr Duong Van Ni said the problem is lack of sediment and that since China built hydropower plants new sand almost never reaches Vietnam. The article says Cambodian sand mining boomed over the last 10 years, partly due to Singapore demand, and that Cambodia banned all sand exports in 2017 under pressure from environmental groups. Ben Tre officials describe unlicensed night-time sand miners, and a local group says it drove off 90 per cent of thieves in the first few months using slingshots and catapults. Singapore's ministry said it imports sand commercially and requires suppliers to comply with source-country laws; China's Foreign Ministry responded about downstream concerns.
records.limitations: News report relying on quoted officials, experts and local residents; figures are attributed estimates or claims and not independently verified; no study methodology or precise mining volumes given. Automated English summary; native-language review may be needed.

reviews.reviewReason: The article is substantively about sand mining on the Mekong and Bassac rivers in Cambodia (Roka Koang, Kandal province), covering erosion, livelihoods, licensing and governance, so it is relevant to the basin. It is not about gold mining. The English title matches the original headline exactly. The date "August 29, 2022" appears in the body text as "Story August 29, 2022"; no publisher metadata was supplied. The summary figures (49 licenses, 2,320 hectares, 11.7 and 11.5 million m3, 6.1 million m3, 4%, 5x, 16x, 5 m, 9,450 m3) are all quoted verbatim in the article, and the allegations and denials are attributed. Two things to note: the article text is truncated mid-sentence, and the draft's "2,320 hectares (5,730 hectares)" figure is quoted as printed. No archive record is the same incident: MSW-442 is a different Khmer-language piece of the same date, and MSW-585 and MSW-800 cover the Dipola press conference rather than this article.

reviews.reviewReason: Reuters/Straits Times article is substantively about sand mining (legal and illegal) and upstream dams causing sediment loss, erosion and subsidence in the Mekong Delta (Ben Tre, Vietnam). It is clearly within the Mekong basin and the title is identical to the original English headline. It is not about gold. The date is supported by the exact quote 'Published Jan 14, 2019, 09:12 AM' and matches the publisher metadata. Figures are attributed to experts, officials and a local patrol member, and the draft's quotes support them. One caveat: the draft's figure quote 'a government ban of all Cambodian sand exports in 2017' and 'over the last 10 years' are verbatim fragments. Countries (Vietnam, Cambodia, China, Laos, Myanmar, Thailand) are supported by the text describing the river's course. No same-incident duplicate: nearby records such as MSW-763 (Ben Tre directive) and MSW-768 (three boats caught on the Tien River) concern different events, and MSW-828 is a different article.
